title: Mass of two objects using a beam balance
objective: To determine the mass of two different objects using a physical beam balance.
To find the resting point of the balance from the turning points of the pointer.
To correct for the zero error of the balance and use its sensitivity.

theory.statement: A beam balance does not measure mass directly. It compares the moment of the unknown body about the central knife edge with the moment of known weights on the other pan. When the beam is horizontal the two moments are equal, and if the arms are of equal length the two masses are equal. This is a null method: the instrument tells you only that two quantities match.
theory.derivationNote: Taking moments about the central knife edge, m·g·a₁ = M·g·a₂, where a₁ and a₂ are the arm lengths. If a₁ = a₂ then m = M, and note that g cancels — a balance compares masses, not weights, and would give the same answer on the Moon. A real beam does not come to rest quickly, so the resting point is found from the swing. The pointer is read at successive turning points, three on one side and two on the other; the mean of the three and the mean of the two are averaged. Taking an odd number on one side and an even number on the other is what makes the steady decay of the amplitude cancel. If the resting point with the load is R and with the pans empty is R₀, the excess mass still needed is (R − R₀) divided by the sensitivity S, the number of divisions the pointer moves per milligram of excess. The mass is then the weights in the pan plus this small correction, which is how a balance can resolve better than its smallest weight.
keyEquations: m·g·a₁ = M·g·a₂, so m = M when a₁ = a₂
Resting point R = ½[mean of odd turning points + mean of even turning points]
Sensitivity S = divisions moved per milligram of excess load
With unequal arms, true mass = √(M₁ × M₂) by double weighing

apparatus.name: Physical beam balance
apparatus.spec: with pointer, scale and beam-raising lever
apparatus.why: Compares the moments of the unknown body and the known weights

apparatus.name: Weight box
apparatus.spec: gram weights with fractional weights down to 10 mg, with forceps
apparatus.why: Provides the known masses that balance the body

apparatus.name: Forceps
apparatus.why: Weights must never be handled with fingers, which add grease and moisture

apparatus.name: Bodies to be weighed
apparatus.why: The unknown masses; the practical requires two

apparatus.name: Spirit level
apparatus.why: The balance must be levelled or the beam will not be horizontal at balance

procedure.text: Level the balance with its screws until the pointer swings equally on both sides of the centre of the scale.
With both pans empty, raise the beam and note five turning points of the pointer. Calculate the resting point; this is the zero of the balance.
Lower the beam. Place the first body on the left pan and add gram weights to the right pan with forceps, starting with a weight you know is too large and halving.
Add fractional weights until the pointer swings about the centre of the scale.
Raise the beam gently and note five turning points, three on one side and two on the other.
Calculate the resting point and hence the mass, using the sensitivity of the balance for the fraction still unaccounted for.
Repeat the whole weighing at least three times.
Remove the first body and repeat the entire procedure for the second body.
Report both masses, corrected for the zero of the balance.

steps: Resting point = ½[mean of turning points 1, 3, 5 + mean of turning points 2, 4]
Zero of the balance = resting point with both pans empty
Excess = (resting point − zero) divided by the sensitivity, in mg
Mass = gram weights + fractional weights + excess
Mean of the trials gives the mass of the body

expectedResult.statement: Body A has a mass of about 24.386 g and body B about 57.142 g. The balance resolves better than the smallest weight in the box because the residual offset of the pointer is converted into milligrams through the sensitivity of the instrument.

safety: Always lower the beam before adding or removing anything from a pan; loading a swinging beam damages the knife edges.
Handle weights only with the forceps provided. Fingers leave grease and moisture, and the weights then read heavy.
Do not exceed the rated capacity of the balance.
Close the balance case, if there is one, before taking the final reading, so that draughts do not disturb the beam.
Return every weight to its correct slot in the box so that the set stays complete.
sourcesOfError: Unequal arms give a constant proportional error which a single weighing cannot reveal.
Zero error of the balance, if the unloaded resting point is not at the centre of the scale.
Weights themselves may be worn or corroded and no longer of their marked value.
Air currents and vibration of the bench disturb the swing.
Buoyancy of the air acts on the body and on the weights differently if their densities differ.
Friction or dust at the knife edges makes the beam sluggish, so it does not come to its true resting point.

viva.question: Why is a beam balance called a null instrument?
viva.expectedConcept: Because it does not display a value. It only indicates whether the moments on the two sides are equal, that is whether the difference is null. The number comes from the known weights the observer chose, not from the instrument.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the pointer scale reads the mass directly.

viva.question: Would a beam balance give the same reading on the Moon?
viva.expectedConcept: Yes. Taking moments, m·g·a = M·g·a, and g cancels from both sides. A beam balance compares masses, so it is unaffected by the value of g. A spring balance, which measures weight, would read differently.
viva.answerLogic: g cancels in the moment equation.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming every weighing instrument depends on gravity in the same way.

viva.question: What is the resting point, and why is it not simply where the pointer stops?
viva.expectedConcept: It is the position about which the pointer would finally settle, found from the centre of its swing. Waiting for a real beam to stop takes a very long time because the damping is small, so the resting point is calculated from the turning points instead.
viva.commonMisconception: Trying to stop the pointer by hand, which introduces a force.

viva.question: Why are three turning points taken on one side and two on the other?
viva.expectedConcept: The amplitude decreases steadily as the swing dies away. Taking an odd number on one side and an even number on the other, and averaging the two means, makes this steady decay cancel out. Averaging all five equally would not.
viva.answerLogic: The asymmetric count cancels the damping.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the numbers three and two are arbitrary convention.

viva.question: What is the sensitivity of a balance?
viva.expectedConcept: The number of scale divisions the resting point shifts for each milligram of excess load in one pan. A higher sensitivity means a larger shift for the same excess, so smaller mass differences can be detected.
viva.commonMisconception: Confusing sensitivity with the capacity of the balance.

viva.question: How can a balance give a mass finer than the smallest weight in the box?
viva.expectedConcept: The pointer will not sit exactly at the zero when the finest available weight has been added. The residual offset, divided by the sensitivity, gives the extra mass in milligrams, and this is added to the weights in the pan.
viva.answerLogic: Convert the pointer offset into mass through the sensitivity.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing the resolution can never be better than the smallest weight.

viva.question: The arms of a balance are slightly unequal. How would you still obtain the correct mass?
viva.expectedConcept: By double weighing. Weigh the body in the left pan to get M₁, then interchange the body and the weights and weigh again to get M₂. The true mass is the geometric mean, √(M₁M₂). The two arm-length errors then cancel.
viva.answerLogic: Method of double weighing, geometric mean.
viva.commonMisconception: Taking the arithmetic mean, which is only approximately right.

viva.question: Why must weights be handled with forceps?
viva.expectedConcept: Fingers deposit grease, moisture and salt on the weights. These add a small but real mass, and over time they corrode the surface, so the weights no longer have their marked values. The error is systematic and affects everyone who later uses that box.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking it is only about keeping the weights looking clean.

viva.question: Why should the beam be lowered before changing the load on a pan?
viva.expectedConcept: The whole beam rests on sharp knife edges, which are what make the balance sensitive. Placing a load on a raised beam gives them a sudden jolt that blunts them, and a blunted knife edge permanently reduces the sensitivity of the instrument.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking it is only to stop the pans swinging about.

viva.question: Two bodies of the same mass but very different densities are weighed in air. Are the readings identical?
viva.expectedConcept: Not exactly. Each body is buoyed up by the weight of the air it displaces, and the larger, less dense body displaces more air, so it appears slightly lighter. For ordinary laboratory work the difference is negligible, but it matters in precision metrology.
viva.answerLogic: Archimedes' principle applies in air too.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming buoyancy only applies to liquids.

preLab.question: A beam balance compares:
options: Weights, so it depends on g
Masses, because g cancels from both sides
preLab.feedback: m·g·a = M·g·a. The g cancels, so a beam balance compares masses and works the same anywhere.

preLab.question: The resting point of a beam balance is found by:
options: Holding the pointer at the centre
Averaging the turning points of the swing
Reading the pointer once at random
preLab.feedback: The swing decays slowly, so the resting point is calculated from the turning points instead of waiting.

preLab.question: Weights must be handled with forceps because:
options: They are too hot to touch
Fingers add grease and moisture, changing their mass
preLab.feedback: Contamination from fingers changes the value of the standard weights permanently.

duringLab.question: Complete at least three full weighings.
Weigh two different bodies, as the practical requires.

postLab.question: State the mass of body A in gram.
postLab.feedback: About 24.386 g, using the sensitivity to resolve the last few milligrams.

postLab.question: State the mass of body B in gram.
Repeating a weighing many times on a balance with unequal arms will:
options: Not remove it, because the error is systematic
postLab.feedback: Unequal arms shift every reading the same way. Only a change of method — double weighing — removes a systematic error.

scientificValidation.formula: m·g·a₁ = M·g·a₂; R = ½[mean(odd T.P.) + mean(even T.P.)]; mass = M + (R − R₀)/S
assumptions: The two arms of the beam are of equal length
The pointer reads at the centre of the scale with both pans empty
The weights are of their marked values and are handled with forceps
Readings are taken while the beam swings freely
Buoyancy of the air is neglected
scientificValidation.validRange: Load 0 to 200 g; fractional weights to 10 mg; sensitivity 1.5 to 2.4 divisions per mg; pointer scale ±10 divisions
scientificValidation.unitSystem: Masses in gram; sensitivity in divisions per milligram
edgeCases: A large excess drives the pointer off the scale and no resting point exists
Unequal arms give a systematic proportional error
A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount
Removing the body altogether measures the zero of the balance, not a mass
Turning points decay steadily, so the odd-even averaging is required
expectedBehaviour: The recovered mass matches the true mass to within a few milligrams
A more sensitive balance gives a larger pointer shift for the same excess
The zero error is corrected out and does not appear in the final mass
The balance refuses to give a reading when the pointer is off the scale
